title.narrative: GSD/UPB/Plastic Smart and Waste Wise Cities in South East Asia

description.narrative:
Rapid urbanization and economic growth have led to increasing waste generation. An estimated 2 billion tonnes of municipal solid waste were generated in 2016, and this number is expected to grow to 3.4 billion tonnes by 2050. Uncontrolled disposal sites are a major source of Green House Gases (GHG), and in a ‘business as usual’ scenario, the waste sector, particularly food waste, is predicted to account for 8-10% of global anthropogenic GHG emission by 2025. Additionally, every year at least 8 million tonnes of plastic find its way into the world’s oceans, harming wildlife, endangering public health, and causing costs for tourist and fishing industries. On the other hand, waste management offers great opportunities: resource recovery lessens the dependency on resource imports and reduces natural resource extraction; it enhances livelihoods and income for the urban poor through new business models; and improves quality of life for urban citizens. In 2018, UN-Habitat, launched Waste Wise Cities with a call to action to address the global challenge of waste management, and encourage cities to be Waste Wise: a city that uses precious resources wisely through rethinking, refusing, reducing, reusing, and recycling its materials and waste before as well as after consumption. Currently more than 200 cities have joined the initiative. Under the Waste Wise Cities programme, UN-Habitat developed the Waste Wise Cities Tool (WaCT), a diagnostic tool that assesses a city’s municipal solid waste management performance through SDG indicator 11.6.1, proportion of MSW collected and managed in controlled facilities, out of total MSW generated by city. WWF’s Plastic Smart Cities initiative supports a no plastic in nature agenda. The initiative has supported cities and coastal centers in taking bold action to stop plastic pollution, with a goal to reduce plastic leakage into nature by 30% by 2025. 25 Asian cities and tourist destinations have joined WWF and the Plastics Smart Cities initiative as pilot cities. During the 10th World Urban Forum in Abu Dhabi, UN-Habitat and WWF International signed a Memorandum of Understanding to tackle the global challenges of waste management and plastic pollution. This project is an outcome of the two agencies’ collaboration to support selected South East Asian cities in becoming “Plastic Smart” and “Waste Wise”, through evidence-based decision making to prevent plastic leakage from their municipal solid waste management system.
UN-Habitat will support WWF offices (in Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam) in building capacity on evidence-based solid waste management action planning of the cities involved in WWF’s Plastic Smart Cities Initiative in South East Asia, namely Bogor, Depok, Jakarta in Indonesia, Manila in the Philippines, Hatyai, Ko Samui, Songklah, and Surat Thani in Thailand and Hue in Vietnam. This will be done through online training of the WWF staff, 3rd party consultants and municipality staff of the selected cities on the Waste Wise Cities Tool (WaCT). Furthermore, UN-Habitat will remotely support WWF, 3rd party consultants and the municipality staff when they apply the WaCT and ensure the quality of the data collection and analysis. UN-Habitat will then remotely support the development and assure the quality of City Action Plans in each city, provide support for the development of monitoring frameworks for these City Action Plans, ensure the integration of the proposed actions with other on-going initiatives, and finally contribute to documentation and dissemination of lessons learnt.
